finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id never enforces the authorize() check because the call is not awaited, so the Promise rejection with 403 is unobserved and the handler deletes the report anyway. Any caller, including one with no delete grant, can delete any report.
finding.source: Authenticated (or any) request to DELETE /reports/:id; req.user is set from req.session.user at server.js:5 with no further guard.

trace.note: Middleware sets req.user = req.session.user; no auth guard on the route.
report loaded by req.params.id with no ownership check.
authorize(req.user, 'delete', report) is called without await. It returns a Promise, which is ignored.
Inside authorize, db.grants resolves asynchronously; the 403 rejection at lines 11-14 happens after the handler has already continued.
remove runs regardless of the authorization result.

finding.guards_checked: Session middleware (lines 4-7) only sets req.user. authorize() (lines 9-16) is correct on its own but its result is discarded. Compared with PUT at line 27, which does await. No route-level or global auth middleware exists in this file. Caveat: Node 15+ defaults to crashing on unhandled rejections, so the 403 may crash the process, possibly before or after the delete commits, depending on DB timing and any app-level unhandledRejection handler. Either outcome is a security failure: unauthorized deletion if the handler survives, and a request-triggered crash (DoS) if it does not.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. The only candidate guard, authorize() (server.js:9-16), throws on failure, but its call at server.js:20 is a bare statement with no await or catch, so the rejection is discarded. The PUT handler at server.js:27 does await it, which shows the intended pattern was not applied to DELETE. No route-level or global auth middleware exists in server.js; the only middleware (lines 4-7) just copies req.session.user.
verdict.reason: At server.js:20 the un-awaited authorize() call is a bare statement, so its 403 throw never gates the db.reports.remove() call at server.js:21, which is issued synchronously before the grant lookup at server.js:10 resolves. Any request that reaches the route with a session object can delete the report. The "any caller" wording overreaches: if req.session is undefined, server.js:5 throws first, so the realistic attacker is any session-holding user, and the crash caveat means the process may die after the delete is issued.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire request body to db.reports.update, which allows mass assignment. A user with only 'write' on a report can set any column the update accepts, such as owner_id or tenant_id, which could transfer ownership or escalate privilege.
finding.source: Request JSON body via express.json() (line 3), under a 'write' grant on the target report.

trace.note: express.json() parses the body into req.body with no field allowlist.
await authorize(req.user, 'write', report) correctly gates the call.
req.body is passed unfiltered to update().

finding.guards_checked: The 'write' grant check at line 27 is correct. There is no field allowlist or schema validation. The db module is not in the repo, so I could not confirm which columns update() writes. Severity depends on the schema: it is only a privilege escalation if owner_id, grants, or similar fields are writable.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws a 403 when the 'write' grant is missing, and line 27 awaits it, so only callers with 'write' on the report reach line 28. No field allowlist or schema validation exists between req.body (server.js:3, 28) and the update call.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: express.json() at server.js:3 fills req.body, the throwing authorize() at server.js:27 gates the call, and req.body goes unfiltered into db.reports.update at server.js:28. Whether an attacker with only 'write' can change owner_id or tenant_id depends on the db module, which is not in the repo, so the privilege-escalation impact cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: With no session user, authorize() reads user.id from undefined and throws a TypeError. Because the handler is async and Express 4 does not catch promise rejections, the rejection is unhandled and can crash the process. An unauthenticated request can trigger this.
finding.source: Request with no session user (no session cookie, or a session without user), reaching PUT or DELETE.
finding.sink: Unhandled promise rejection in the route handler (server.js:18-30)

trace.note: req.user becomes undefined when the session has no user.
user.id throws a TypeError inside authorize().
In PUT the handler awaits authorize() (line 27), so the rejection is not caught by any try/catch and propagates out of the async handler.

finding.guards_checked: No try/catch or error middleware for async handlers. Express 4 does not forward async rejections to next(). Lower severity than F1: it is a crash/DoS, not an access bypass. Depends on the Express version and the unhandled-rejection setting.

verdict.guard_found: none. There is no try/catch or error middleware around the async handlers (server.js:18-30), and the only middleware (server.js:4-7) just copies req.session.user. The authorize() call on line 20 is not awaited, which is a second unhandled-rejection path that the candidate did not mention.
verdict.reason: At server.js:9-10, authorize() evaluates user.id before any await, so an anonymous request whose req.session.user is undefined (server.js:5) rejects, and nothing catches it at server.js:26-27 or 18-20. The crash depends on two conditions the file does not show: a session middleware must set req.session (absent that, server.js:5 throws synchronously and Express returns a 500 with no crash), and the app must run on Express 4 with Node's default unhandled-rejection crash, since no package.json is present to confirm the version.
